Ami Vora Mike Krieger Product Management Anthropic Claude AI Why Claude Can’t Be Your PM (Yet)? Sam Kirubaharan 7 min read · Oct 3, 2026 -- Listen Share Before we begin, let’s start with the bugging question. Is everyone a PM in the AI era? You don’t have to carry the title “Product Manager” to increasingly work like one. But you should act as one. AI is making it dramatically easier to turn an idea into something tangible. You can explore a problem, build a prototype, test an approach, get feedback, iterate and try again — often without waiting for a large team or a long development cycle. That changes the role of the person with the idea. When building becomes easier, more people can participate in deciding what should be built, why it should exist, who it should serve and how it should evolve. In that sense, the AI era is making product thinking accessible far beyond the traditional PM role. At the Lenny & Friends Summit, Anthropic’s Ami Vora and Mike Krieger joined Dan Shipper to discuss how product management is changing as AI capabilities evolve rapidly. Why Claude Can’t Be Your PM (Yet)? The conversation covered the changing role of PMs, agent-native software, experimentation, product-market fit, and what happens when the technology changes faster than traditional product development cycles. Here are seven important questions from the discussion. 1. If AI can build almost anything, what becomes the PM’s real job? The fundamental role of product remains the same: bridging real problems people have with technology that can solve them. What has changed is the speed of technological change. Technology that once evolved over five or ten years can now change every couple of months. The human side, however, does not change at the same pace. People continue to have many of the same underlying problems and needs. This creates a different responsibility for product leaders. They need to remain deeply focused on the human problem while continuously updating their understanding of what the technology can do. The ability to discard previous assumptions becomes important. A solution that worked with yesterday’s technology may no longer be the right solution today. Product teams need to understand the problem deeply while being willing to reconsider how that problem should be solved as capabilities change. As AI makes building easier and faster, the number of possible things to build also expands. That makes product judgment increasingly important: determining what should be built , rather than simply determining whether something can be built. 2. Why can’t Claude simply be the PM? Mike Krieger described a recent experience that changed his view of the PM role. He had moved into an individual-contributor role focused primarily on building. As a project approached launch, a PM lead pointed out that the project still needed a PM. Initially, Mike questioned whether that was necessary. Claude was already involved in the work, and there were many AI-assisted workflows operating around the project. But the PM role became visible through everything that could otherwise have been missed. Someone needed to consider how different customer groups would be brought along. Customer success needed to understand upcoming changes. Safeguards needed to be involved. Teams needed to remain aligned. Dependencies needed to be connected. The PM provided the glue and connective tissue across all of these activities. Claude can already identify connections and surface information across an organization. But the panel distinguished this from being a convenor — someone who brings people together, creates organizational pull and makes sure the right people are connected to move the work forward. That organizational role remains important even as AI takes on more of the work itself. 3. Which traditional PM skills are becoming less valuable? One of the biggest changes is the economics of deciding before building. Ami Vora described spending much of her career developing intuition around product and interaction design. Product reviews could involve detailed discussions about where a button should be placed, how an interaction should work, and what a user would do in a particular situation. That expertise was valuable when building and shipping software was expensive. With AI-assisted development, it can sometimes be faster to build several versions and see what works. Instead of spending a large amount of time predicting the correct interaction beforehand, a team can build three versions, put them in front of users, and learn from the results. The underlying product and design questions have not disappeared. What has changed is the cost of answering them. The shift is from predicting the right answer before building toward building quickly enough to discover the answer through experimentation . This also creates a personal version of the innovator’s dilemma. People can become attached to the skills that made them successful in the past, even when the technology has changed the relative value of those skills. 4. What becomes more important for PMs?
